newsitem.title: USA: Mars remarkably like Earth, rock analysis finds.
newsitem.headline: Mars remarkably like Earth, rock analysis finds.

text.p: Mars is more similar to the Earth in its composition than even the moon, startled scientists announced on Tuesday after studying the results of the first-ever robotic analysis of a Martian rock.

In addition, they said, the analysis went a long way towards proving that a meteorite believed to have come from Mars and thought to contain fossil evidence of ancient life did indeed come from the Red Planet.

What the Mars Pathfinder spacecraft's little rover, Sojourner, found when it scanned a rock known as "Barnacle Bill" with its alpha proton X-ray spectrometer was that it was probably one third quartz in composition because of the amount of silica it contained.

"I was just floored when it came out silica and I am still struggling with what the implications are. This is more like Earth than our own moon, which has no quartz on it," said Hap McSween of the University of Tennessee, a participating scientist in the Pathfinder science project.

The rover's analysis also revealed the rock's "chemical fingerprints" which McSween said were identical to the 12 meteorites found on Earth that scientists believed originated on Mars billions of years ago.
"So now we can say we have analysed 13 Martian rocks," he said during a press briefing at NASA's Jet Propulsion laboratory here.

One of the 12 meteorites examined -- designated ALH80041 and discovered in Alaska -- was examined with new techniques two years ago by scientists from NASA and Stanford University in California and was found to contain organic molecules and iron mineral compounds commonly associated with microscopic organisms.
McSween said there were three ways that quartz was formed; by volcanoes, by a rock melting on impact and then cooling, or by water creating it from sediment.

All three were possibilities, he said, pointing out that there was a crater near the landing site and there was evidence, announced on Monday, that the area was scene of a catastrophic flood billions of years ago.
McSween said scientists would have a better idea how the rock was formed after studying high resolution, close-up photographs of the rock due to be downloaded to Earth Tuesday night.
If it turned out be a volcanic product, McSween said, it would be a lava called Andesite, named after lava crusts found in the Andes and the second-most common form of lava found on Earth.
"This is a real surprise. We were not expecting to find a rock of this composition," McSween added.
He said the other two elements making up the rock were feldspar, the most common mineral in Earth's crust, and orthopyroxene, another mineral commonly found in Earth rocks.
McSween said that while the spectrometer was not designed to detect quartz, he was certain it was present because, "We haven't seen this much silica in rocks on Earth that didn't contain quartz."
The rover scanned "Barnacle Bill" for 10 hours on Sunday, bombarding it with protons and recording the changes in them as they bounced back to the instrument.

Mission Scientist Matthew Golombek said the Sojourner had also performed "the first wheelies on Mars" during a "soil mechanics experiment" that called for the rover to lock all its wheels except the middle ones and then spin the middle ones to kick up the red Martian dust to determine how firm or loose the surface layer was.

Golombek said as of Monday night, Pathfinder had sent back more than 1,175 images since it landed in the Ares Vallis basin of Mars last Friday. "The more we look at this site the more we are amazingly happy at the wide variety of (rock) samples we are seeing. I could only hope for this in my wildest dreams," he added.
"This site literally is a rock festival," deadpanned McSween. "A smorgasbord of rocks is what we have here."

Rudolph Rieder of the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Germany and the Principal Spectrometer Investigator, said things had gone so well at the landing site, "that some people might believe this is a hoax. We can assure you it is not a hoax."
